questions.q: What is the first program that executes when a computer is powered on, and where is it stored?
questions.a: The first program is the firmware (BIOS or UEFI), stored in a non-volatile ROM chip on the motherboard. A wrong answer like "Windows loader" or "kernel" reveals the student thinks the OS loads directly, missing the firmware's role as the hardware initializer.

questions.q: Explain why a warm boot is faster than a cold boot, referencing the specific steps that are skipped.
questions.a: Warm boot skips the Power-On Self-Test (POST), hardware enumeration, and peripheral initialization because the CPU and devices are already in a known powered state. It jumps directly to the firmware's bootloader handoff. If a student says "warm boot skips loading the OS," they confuse warm boot with hibernate/resume; warm boot still reloads the OS kernel.

questions.q: A user reports that after a sudden power loss, their computer takes longer to start and shows a "Press F1 to continue" message. Identify the boot type and the likely cause of the message.
questions.a: This is a cold boot triggered by power loss. The message appears because the CMOS battery failed, causing BIOS settings (date/time, boot order) to reset; POST detects the checksum mismatch and halts. A wrong answer attributing the delay to "OS corruption" misses the hardware-level POST and CMOS role.

questions.q: Compare the boot process on a system with UEFI firmware versus legacy BIOS, focusing on where the bootloader is located and how it is loaded.
questions.a: UEFI reads bootloader files (e.g., .efi) from an EFI System Partition (ESP) on GPT disks using a built-in file system driver; legacy BIOS reads the first 446 bytes of the Master Boot Record (MBR) on the first disk sector. A student saying "both use MBR" shows they haven't grasped the partitioning scheme difference.

questions.q: A school lab has 30 identical PCs. The IT admin wants to reduce the time students wait for computers to become ready after a scheduled restart. Evaluate whether configuring "Fast Startup" (hybrid boot) in Windows achieves this for warm boots, and justify your answer.
questions.a: Fast Startup saves the kernel session to disk during shutdown (hibernation-like) and restores it on next boot, making cold boots faster. It does not affect warm boots (restarts) because a restart performs a full cold boot sequence. A student claiming it speeds up restarts misunderstands that Fast Startup only applies to shutdown/startup cycles, not reboots.

questions.q: Design a flowchart that a technician could use to diagnose whether a boot failure occurs during POST, bootloader stage, or kernel loading. Include decision points for beep codes, screen messages, and LED indicators.
questions.a: A good flowchart starts with "Power on → Observe beep codes/LEDs". If beeps/POST codes appear → POST failure. If manufacturer logo appears but no OS logo → bootloader failure (check ESP/MBR). If OS logo appears but hangs → kernel/driver failure. A poor answer that lists only "check cables" shows inability to isolate the boot stage.
